title: In human chromosomes 13-22, neutral repeat DNA with matched primate scores shows most of the gnomAD variant deficit in primate-specific constrained DHS cores, so it cannot confirm their function
abstract: Human populations carry fewer and rarer variants in DNA that a 2024 study called constrained only in primates, but neutral DNA with the same primate conservation scores shows most of the same deficit, so this evidence cannot confirm a primate-specific function. This matters because such calls add a lineage-specific layer to the functional fraction of the human genome, and the primate score is used to rank non-coding variants. Kuderna et al. (Nature 2024) reported 111,318 DNase I hypersensitive sites (DHSs, open-chromatin regions) and 267,410 footprints constrained in primates but not in other mammals, supported by gnomAD-based constraint and reporter assays. On human chromosomes 13-22 (552 Mb of non-coding DNA; gnomAD v4.1, 76,215 genomes; non-CpG variants) we used ancestral repeats (old transposon copies, the usual neutral reference) with matched primate scores as the control. Per base, the score has little power: a base unchanged in 233 primates gets at most P = 0.011, and only 15-27% of mammal-conserved bases reach the cut-off. Among bases without mammal signal, primate calls occur at 0.99 (95% CI 0.98-1.00) times the neutral rate in unannotated DNA and 1.15 (1.13-1.17) times in ENCODE regulatory elements. Primate-specific DHS cores have 6.6% fewer variant sites and 0.76 percentage points more singletons (variants seen once) than DHS cores not called constrained, more than mammal-constrained cores (2.7%, 0.35). Neutral 40-bp windows with the same shift in primate score reproduce 80-133% of this deficit and 72-92% (intervals 39-141%) of the singleton excess across three matching designs. As a positive control, the same correction removes the signal of mammal-constrained cores, so the comparison cannot measure constraint in either direction. In neutral windows the variant deficit rises from -2.4% to 10-13% with the primate score, because the score selects DNA with a low mutation rate that humans share. At single bases, naive tests make primate-specific bases look 0.63 times as constrained as mammal-conserved bases; after subtracting the neutral-repeat signal the ratio is 0.07-0.26 in unannotated DNA (intervals include 0) and 0.15-0.41 in regulatory elements. Limitations: 10 of 22 autosomes; the element test of the paper is approximated by mean window scores; the Gnocchi scores and reporter assays of the paper were not tested.
